title: Do You Need a Frontier Model as a Citation Verifier? Benchmarking Rubric LLMs for Deep-Research Source Attribution
research_question: How capable and expensive must an LLM citation judge be to evaluate source relevance and factual support reliably, and what judge biases are hidden by aggregate accuracy metrics?
methodology: The authors construct the Deep-Research Citation Benchmark from a long-form report spanning 25 topic domains, producing 624 attribution-citation pairs and 1,248 gold rubric decisions for source relevance and factual support. About 60 percent of claims are adversarially edited using 19 perturbation strategies, and a six-model labeling council is followed by human review of every decision, with intensive adjudication of 378 disagreement cases. Eight off-the-shelf LLM judges from three model families are evaluated using pass-class F1, Cohen's kappa, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, pass-rate drift, and bootstrap confidence intervals. The study also compares judge quality with API cost using June 2026 provider pricing.

key_findings.finding: A more expensive frontier judge was not consistently more accurate: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest reported source-relevance F1 at 0.908 despite being among the lower-cost evaluated judges.
For factual support, the 95 percent confidence intervals of all eight judges overlap, so the benchmark does not establish a statistically distinguishable winner on that dimension.
Judge cost spans a 49-fold range in the study, but cost does not track citation-verification accuracy.
Judges with similar aggregate F1 can have materially different pass-rate drift, false-positive rates, and false-negative rates, so scalar F1 hides operationally important directional bias.

All eight judges are systematically stricter than the gold labels on source relevance, and factual-support errors are dominated by rejection of genuinely supported citations rather than acceptance of unsupported ones.
Judge rankings change substantially on the 378 disagreement cases, showing that full-benchmark F1 is an incomplete measure of reliability on ambiguous citation decisions.
key_findings.section: 4 Human Adjudication and 5.4 Reward Noise from Disagreement

key_findings.finding: The paper argues that directional judge biases will shape downstream reinforcement-learning behavior, but that downstream training effect is inferred from the error profile rather than directly demonstrated by an RL training experiment in this study.

limitations: The reported findings are limited to a single adversarial long-form document, even though its contents span 25 topic domains.
Sensitivity to prompt design remains an open question identified by the authors.
Sensitivity to batch-scoring strategies remains an open question identified by the authors.
Two evaluated judges, GPT-5-mini and Claude Opus 4.6, also participate in the gold-label council, although the human-adjudicated subset provides a partially independent check.
The benchmark intentionally contains many adversarial edits and has a low factual-support gold pass rate, so its class distribution may differ substantially from production citation traffic.
Cost comparisons use provider API prices as of June 2026 and therefore are time-dependent.
The source-relevance rubric partly overlaps conceptually with factual support, which the authors identify as a frequent cause of inter-judge disagreement.
raw_claims: The benchmark contains 624 attribution-citation pairs and 1,248 source-relevance and factual-support decisions.
Every gold decision receives human review, and 378 disagreement cases receive additional adjudication.
Eight LLM judges from three model families are evaluated on every benchmark pair.
GPT-5-mini obtains a source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908.
All reported factual-support confidence intervals overlap across the eight judges.
The evaluated judge costs span approximately a 49-fold range.
Judge price does not reliably predict citation-verification performance in this benchmark.
Judges differ substantially in false-positive rate, false-negative rate, and pass-rate drift even when their aggregate F1 scores are similar.
Factual-support judges tend to reject valid support more often than they accept invalid support.
Performance rankings shift on cases where the labeling council originally disagreed.
The authors identify full-set F1 as insufficient for characterizing reliability on the most ambiguous citations.
The conclusions are explicitly limited by use of one adversarial long-form document and unresolved sensitivity to prompting and batching.
